title: Care
hook: a planner filled in on day one, blank by week three; Shantideva's next chapter asks how a vow is kept
tomorrow: what keeps beating us, when it has no hands at all?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the vow. Before all the Buddhas, Shantideva promised to work for the good of every being, and said today my life is fruitful. The promise is made. Now it has to be kept.
screen: `TODAY MY LIFE IS FRUITFUL.` → `NOW, KEEP IT.`

segments.voice: Saturday morning, and a friend posts a photo in the group chat: a brand-new planner, every week color-coded, a promise to herself written on page one in her best handwriting. Everyone sends hearts. A few weeks later the planner is under a pile of mail, open to a page that stays blank. Nobody broke that promise on purpose. It just wasn't guarded. Shantideva knows this moment well. The vow he took yesterday is enormous, and his very next chapter starts right here: now that it's made, how does it stay alive?
screen: `A PLANNER, PAGE ONE.` → `A FEW WEEKS LATER.` → `NOW THAT IT'S MADE?`

segments.voice: Chapter four of the poem is named for one word: apramada, care. Literally, not-careless. The opposite of letting it slide. Shantideva opens it plainly: having firmly taken hold of the awakening mind, a bodhisattva should strive never to stray from it. Then he gets blunt with himself. He invited every being to happiness, out loud, before the Buddhas. If he lets that slide now, he says, he'd be deceiving them all. So the vow isn't a mood that comes and goes. It's a promise with names on it. The Pali form of the same word is appamada, and the Dhammapada gives it a chapter of its own. In Max Müller's old English, that chapter begins: "Earnestness is the path of immortality". Earnestness, care, heedfulness: translators reach for different words, and the picture underneath holds steady. A promise is like a small flame carried across a windy yard. Nobody blames the wind for being wind. You cup your hand. That's the whole teaching of care. It isn't anxiety, and it isn't perfection. It's attention, again and again, to the thing you said you'd do. The next pages name what tries to blow the flame out.
screen: `APRAMADA: NOT-CARELESS.` · `LETTING IT SLIDE DECEIVES THEM ALL.` · `EARNESTNESS, THE PATH.` · `A FLAME IN A WINDY YARD.` · then, large: `GUARD THE VOW.`

segments.voice: Find a pen and anything to write on. Write one promise you've already made, small and real: to a friend, to your body, to yourself. Under it, write the one next step that keeps it this week, and rest your eyes on the page while the sit runs.
Care: apramada, the opposite of careless. Shantideva's name for keeping a vow alive long after the moment of making it.
Keep this one close: guard the vow, the way you'd cup a flame in the wind. Chapter four, begun.

screen: `DAY 1471 COUNTS.` → `SHANTIDEVA'S GUIDE · 16 OF 50.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT KEEPS BEATING US, WHEN IT HAS NO HANDS AT ALL?`

howItsDone: Some Mahayana Buddhists who have taken the bodhisattva vow renew it in their regular chanting, and Shantideva's chapter on care is studied as a guide to keeping that vow day to day.

fork.setup: in june you promised your little cousin you'd teach her to ride a bike this summer. it's august. what does Shantideva's care look like now?
options: wait for a totally free weekend so you can do it properly.
put one short ride on the calendar this week, and show up.
tell her summer got busy, and promise again for next year.
fork.reveal: care isn't a grand gesture someday. it's attention to the promise now, one small, guarded step at a time.

original.note: Sanskrit: care, heedfulness, literally not-carelessness. In Pali the same word is appamada.

trapdoor: what you thought: care means being gentle or nice.
what it means: in Shantideva's chapter four, care is guarding a vow so it doesn't quietly slide.
what a scholar hears: apramada, 'non-carelessness'; its Pali form appamada names a chapter of the Dhammapada, which Max Müller rendered 'earnestness'.
guess: keeping close watch so a promise doesn't slide
being soft and gentle with everyone you meet
worrying about a task until it's done perfectly

chat.says: said yes to painting the school library mural. two weeks. i always flake on big things. how do i not?
options: Guard the yes like a flame: one small piece of the mural every day, starting today.
Wait until you feel really inspired, then knock it all out in one big weekend.
Don't stress. If the mural is meant to happen, it'll get done somehow.
chat.meaning: Shantideva's care: a promise doesn't keep itself. Small, steady attention guards it better than a big push later.

appamada.meaning: the Pali form of the same word: care, earnestness

bodhisattva.meaning: one who vows to wake up for the sake of all beings

Dhammapada.meaning: a collection of the Buddha's sayings in verse

Shantideva.meaning: Buddhist poet-monk who wrote this guide to the bodhisattva's way

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 4.1-4.6 (having firmly grasped the awakening mind, never stray from it; having invited all beings, to fail them would be to deceive them)

sources.quoted: Earnestness is the path of immortality

notes: Chapter 4's title is given as apramada (care, heedfulness); some editions name it bodhicittapramada or 'conscientiousness'. Confirm the chapter name and that 'not-careless' is a fair gloss of the a-pramada formation.
4.1 and the 'deceiving all beings' verses (around 4.4-4.6) are paraphrased; confirm verse numbers for the edition used.

Dhammapada 21, Max Müller 1881: quoted only the opening clause, 'Earnestness is the path of immortality' (his text continues '(Nirvâna), thoughtlessness the path of death'). Please check the exact wording against the 1881 SBE text; also confirm the Pali chapter (Appamadavagga) begins at verse 21.
